responses_by_run.answer: Achilles withdrew from the fighting after his quarrel with Agamemnon because Agamemnon took his prize, Briseis. According to Homer's account, Achilles was angry that Agamemnon threatened to seize his prize despite Achilles bearing the brunt of the furious battle, while Agamemnon's own prize was far greater [1]. In response to this dishonor, Achilles declared he would return home to Phthia rather than remain in the war [1]. Apollodorus similarly reports that Achilles did not go forth to war because he was angry on account of Briseis, the daughter of Chryses the priest [2].

Athena turned Arachne into a spider as punishment for her pride and defiance [1]. Arachne, a mortal weaver of extraordinary skill, refused to acknowledge Athena's superiority in the art of weaving [1]. When Athena appeared to her in disguise as an old woman and advised her to seek the goddess's pardon, Arachne scornfully rejected the advice and challenged the goddess to a weaving contest [1]. After Arachne lost the contest, Athena was enraged not only by Arachne's skill but by her refusal to show proper respect to the goddess [1]. Athena destroyed Arachne's web, struck her repeatedly, and when Arachne attempted to hang herself, Athena saved her life but transformed her into a spider, condemning her to weave forever as eternal punishment for her presumption [1].

responses_by_run.answer: Prometheus was punished for two main transgressions. First, he stole fire and gave it to humans [1]. Second, he attempted to deceive Zeus during a dispute at Mecone by dividing sacrificial portions unfairly [2]. According to Hesiod, Prometheus tried to trick Zeus by presenting him with bones covered in fat while giving the better portions to mortals, and he 'matched himself in wit with the almighty son of Cronos,' which provoked Zeus's wrath [2][3]. When Zeus discovered that Prometheus had hidden fire in a stalk of fennel and given it to humans, he ordered Hephaestus to nail Prometheus to Mount Caucasus, where an eagle devoured his liver daily [1].

Odysseus escaped Polyphemus through a two-part plan. First, he blinded the Cyclops by sharpening a club, heating it in fire, and driving it into Polyphemus's eye with the help of his comrades [1][2]. When Polyphemus cried out for help from other Cyclopes, they misunderstood his cry of "Nobody" and left him alone [1][2]. Second, after the blinding, Odysseus tied the sheep together in groups of three and hid himself beneath the largest ram, clinging to its fleece [3][4]. When Polyphemus opened the cave door to let his flocks out to pasture, he felt the sheep as they passed but could not detect the men hidden beneath them [3][4]. Odysseus and his comrades thus escaped with the sheep to their ships [3][4].

Perseus encountered numerous monsters throughout his adventures. Most notably, he slew the Gorgon Medusa and beheaded her [1][2]. He also encountered Phineus and his fellow conspirators, whom he turned to stone by displaying the Gorgon's head [3][4]. Similarly, he turned Polydectes and his assembled friends to stone using the same weapon [3][4].

During a battle at Seriphus, Perseus engaged and slew several named opponents including Erithus (son of Actor), Caucasian Abaris, Polydaemon, Sperchius, Lycetus, Elyces, Clytus, and Phlegias, along with numerous other unnamed men in Phineus's throng [3][4][5]. Additionally, Perseus encountered the Phorcides, the three old women sisters of the Gorgons [1][2]. Along his journey, he also witnessed men and animals that had been turned to stone by Medusa's deadly gaze [3][4][5].

Zeus's lineage traces back through several divine generations to primordial chaos. Zeus was the son of Cronus [1] and Rhea [2]. Cronus himself was born from Earth (Gaia) and Ouranos [3], the sky deity who represented the earliest divine order. Earth and Ouranos emerged from the primordial cosmos, establishing the genealogical chain that would eventually produce Zeus as king of the gods [1][2][3].
